name: Question 7
problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14068126/assets/4cb2c8128f24adddacd82b5f477848faa47ae52f95a5bb0636a8b286a6628a08.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,{z}^{2}\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height $2$ whose base is a circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,{z}^{2}\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14068126/assets/e6fe01196298c1da0961fd01c73ee4cb7c71b6a03a027cceaba0e68be944c968.png)

 
Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=2$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,{z}^{2}\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,{2}^{2}\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =4\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}4\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =4{∬}_{D}\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(x,y)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4{∬}_{D}\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =4{∬}_{D}\sqrt{16-{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}r\sqrt{16-{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}r\sqrt{16-{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =4\cdot 2\pi \cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}r\sqrt{16-{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}r\sqrt{16-{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=16-{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=-2r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & 2 \\ u & 16 & 12\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}8\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}r\sqrt{16-{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r & =8\pi \cdot {\int }_{16}^{12}\sqrt{u}(-\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{12}^{16}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\pi \cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{12}^{16} \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{3}[64-24\sqrt{3}] \\  & =\frac{64\pi (8-3\sqrt{3})}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
F(x,y,0)=⟨0,\,0,\,{0}^{2}\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{64\pi (8-3\sqrt{3})}{3}+0 \\  & =\frac{64\pi (8-3\sqrt{3})}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

If S is an oriented surface with unit normal vector n, and F is continuous vector field, then the flux of F across S measured with respect to n is given by ∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS.

Notice that only the z-component of F=⟨0,0,z216−x2−y2⟩ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of S is parallel to the z-axis, the flux of F through S will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides.

Let's consider the flux of F through these two sides.

  • Let S1 denote the top surface. On this surface, we have z=2 for x2+y2≤4. The outward-pointing unit normal vector to S1 is n1=⟨0,0,1⟩. Using the fact that z=2 on S1, we have F⋅n1=⟨0,0,z216−x2−y2⟩⋅⟨0,0,1⟩=⟨0,0,2216−x2−y2⟩⋅⟨0,0,1⟩=416−x2−y2. Therefore, the flux of F across S1 is given by ∬S1F⋅dS=∬S1F⋅n1dS=∬S1416−x2−y2dS=4∬D16−x2−y2dA. Applying a change of variables (x,y)→(r,θ),dA=rdrdθ, we have 4∬D16−x2−y2dA=4∬D16−r2rdrdθ=4∫02π∫02r16−r2drdθ=4∫02πdθ∫02r16−r2dr=4⋅2π⋅∫02r16−r2dr=8π∫02r16−r2dr.

Setting u=16−r2, we get du=−2rdr. Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

8π∫02r16−r2dr=8π⋅∫1612u(−12du)=4π∫1216u1/2du=4π⋅23[u3/2]1216=8π3[64−243]=64π(8−33)3.

  • Let S2 denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have z=0 for x2+y2≤4. Therefore, for everywhere on S2, we have F(x,y,0)=⟨0,0,0216−x2−y2⟩=⟨0,0,0⟩. Therefore, ∬S2F⋅ndS=∬S20⋅ndS=∬S20dS=0.

Finally, ∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS=∬S1F⋅ndS+∬S2F⋅ndS=64π(8−33)3+0=64π(8−33)3.
